metadata.note: The electric interurban network the North Shore Railroad built in southern Marin County, California, and the Northwestern Pacific ran until 1941: third-rail (600 V DC) trains from the Sausalito ferry terminal, where boats connected to San Francisco, to Mill Valley, to San Rafael by two routes (via San Anselmo, and via the Baltimore Park cutoff and Green Brae), and to Fairfax and Manor. Opened 21 August 1903 (Mill Valley) and 17 October 1903 (San Rafael via San Anselmo); Green Brae route 1904; San Anselmo-Manor 1908; all service ended 28 February 1941. The four services are drawn as four routes, each the way a passenger rode it from Sausalito, so the Sausalito-San Anselmo trunk is drawn more than once - that overlap is real (trains for San Rafael and Manor ran coupled to San Anselmo). Each route is split at the 1907 merger into the Northwestern Pacific.
metadata.colour_note: North Shore Railroad #7FA650 (new, pre-reserved for this batch; checked unused anywhere in data/). Northwestern Pacific Railroad #386641, reused programmatically from data/northwestern_pacific_santa_rosa.geojson.
metadata.ownership_note: Rule 4 split at 1907, when the North Shore was merged into the Northwestern Pacific and NWP began running the trains. Deliberately NOT a split at April 1904, when E. H. Harriman (Southern Pacific) bought the North Shore: he owned the stock, but the North Shore kept operating its trains under its own name until 1907. Also not split at 1929, when the Southern Pacific bought the Santa Fe's half of the NWP: the NWP remained the operating company.
metadata.scope_note: Only electric passenger years are drawn. Deliberately left out: the North Pacific Coast's narrow-gauge steam service on the same lines before 1903 (a different topic, not sourced here); the planned but never-built electrification of San Rafael-San Quentin; NWP steam trains beyond Manor to Point Reyes and Cazadero; Tiburon-line trains (already in data/northwestern_pacific_santa_rosa.geojson); and the San Rafael-Sausalito trackage after 1941, which carried freight only until abandoned in 1972 (Rule 1). The Sausalito ferries are not rail and are not drawn.
metadata.mode_note: mode 'interurban' (Rule 7): electric multiple-unit trains linking separate towns - Sausalito, Mill Valley, Corte Madera, Larkspur, San Anselmo, Fairfax, San Rafael - on private right of way with a ferry connection; Wikipedia classes it as an interurban.
metadata.geometry_quality: All four routes are traced; there are no straight-line legs. About 70% of the drawn length is OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=Northwestern Pacific Railroad (the abandoned grade, mostly rail-trails: Mill Valley - Sausalito Path, Larkspur Path, Corte Madera - Larkspur Path, Alto Tunnel) or the SMART main line on the old formation. The rest is OpenHistoricalMap (CC0) ways digitised from the USGS 1895/1897 topographic sheets - coarse but real: the Sausalito waterfront (1.7 mi), the Mill Valley branch (1.7 mi) and the San Anselmo-San Rafael branch (about 2 mi, the weakest piece). OHM dates were NOT used. Traced vs documented (1933 timetable) mileage: Mill Valley 5.2/5.2, San Rafael via San Anselmo 12.8/12.5, San Rafael via Green Brae 10.6/10.5, Manor 12.3/12.3 (cut to length). Despike/reversal/revisit checks run; 7 reversal vertices at fragment joins near San Anselmo removed.

Sausalito ferry terminal to Waldo (first ~1.7 mi): OpenHistoricalMap way 200221493 (CC0, digitised from the USGS Tamalpais 1897 topographic sheet) - real but coarse, about one vertex per 150-300 m along the Sausalito waterfront, which has been built over. Waldo to Almonte, Alto tunnel, Corte Madera and Baltimore Park: OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=Northwestern Pacific Railroad (Mill Valley - Sausalito Path, Alto Tunnel, Corte Madera Pathway), i.e. the abandoned NWP grade itself. segments.note: The North Shore Railroad (the North Pacific Coast, renamed 7 March 1902 under John Martin and Eugene de Sabla) standard-gauged and electrified the Sausalito-San Anselmo main line and the Almonte-Mill Valley branch with 600 V DC third rail; electric revenue service began Sausalito-Mill Valley on 21 August 1903 (Wikipedia citing Trimble 1977 p.71; the North Pacific Coast article, citing Demoro 1983, gives 20 August - source conflict recorded). Trains met the Sausalito ferries to San Francisco. E. H. Harriman (Southern Pacific) bought the North Shore in April 1904, but the North Shore kept operating under its own name until it was merged into the Northwestern Pacific in 1907, so this feature keeps the North Shore colour to 1907. The pre-1903 narrow-gauge steam service on the branch (opened 1889) is not drawn. Headway is an ESTIMATE (trains timed to the Sausalito ferries, roughly half-hourly at peaks).
sources: Segment-level: dates from Wikipedia (citing Trimble, Interurban Railways of the Bay Area, 1977, pp.67-74) and Sievers, Western Railroader Aug 1954; headway is an estimate, not sourced.

properties.line: North Shore: Sausalito – San Rafael (via San Anselmo)
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE carried back from the 1933 NWP timetable (12.5 mi in 32 min for an all-stops train, about 37 km/h); no North Shore-era timetable was checked.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 12.8 mi against a documented 12.5 mi (1933 employee timetable: Sausalito 6.5, San Anselmo 16.5, West End 17.9, B Street 18.5, San Rafael 19.0). Sausalito ferry terminal to Waldo (first ~1.7 mi): OpenHistoricalMap way 200221493 (CC0, digitised from the USGS Tamalpais 1897 topographic sheet) - real but coarse, about one vertex per 150-300 m along the Sausalito waterfront, which has been built over. Waldo to Almonte, Alto tunnel, Corte Madera and Baltimore Park: OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=Northwestern Pacific Railroad (Mill Valley - Sausalito Path, Alto Tunnel, Corte Madera Pathway), i.e. the abandoned NWP grade itself. Baltimore Park to San Anselmo: OSM NWP-tagged abandoned grade (Larkspur Path, Magnolia Avenue, College Avenue, Sylvan Lane and untagged NWP grade), with one 0.2 mi OHM fill near Ross where OSM has a gap. San Anselmo to San Rafael, about 2.7 mi traced against a documented 2.5: APPROXIMATE - OpenHistoricalMap way 200221496 (USGS 1897 topo, only 14 vertices for the whole San Anselmo-San Rafael-San Quentin branch), joined to a short OSM NWP fragment and the SMART main line for the last 0.4 mi into the San Rafael depot; expect the drawn line to sit up to ~100 m off the real grade through West End and B Street. Connectors between fragments total 0.4 mi, the longest 0.17 mi. Milepost check against the 1933 employee timetable (distances from San Francisco; Sausalito = 6.5): traced Almonte 10.0 (TT 9.9), Larkspur 13.3 (13.4), Ross 15.7 (15.5), San Anselmo 16.5 (16.5), San Rafael 19.3 (19.0). ERA CAVEAT for the North Shore feature: from October 1903 until the 1904 Baltimore Park cutoff the North Shore's San Rafael trains used the old North Pacific Coast San Rafael station, not the California Northwestern depot; this feature draws the post-1904 run-in to the CNW depot for the whole North Shore era (a difference of well under 1 mi at the end of the line). The exact 1903 terminal site is not sourced.

segments.note: Electric service from Sausalito over the newly double-tracked, dual-gauge main line through the Alto tunnel, Corte Madera, Larkspur, Kentfield and Ross to San Anselmo, then over the old North Pacific Coast San Rafael branch, began 17 October 1903 (Wikipedia citing Trimble p.71; North Pacific Coast article citing Demoro). It was the first third-rail electrification in California and used the first alternating-current track-circuit signals (Union Switch & Signal, Sausalito-San Anselmo, 1903 - Sievers). Harriman bought the North Shore in April 1904; it ran its own trains until merged into the Northwestern Pacific in 1907. Headway is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: dates from Wikipedia (citing Trimble 1977) and the North Pacific Coast Railroad article (citing Demoro 1983); headway is an estimate, not sourced.

properties.line: North Shore: Sausalito – San Rafael (via Green Brae)
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE carried back from the 1933 NWP timetable (10.5 mi in 18 min, about 56 km/h, for the limited-stop cutoff trains), reduced for the North Shore era; no North Shore-era timetable was checked.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 10.6 mi against a documented 10.5 mi (1933 employee timetable: Sausalito 6.5, Almonte 9.9, Baltimore Park 13.0, California Park 15.7, San Rafael 17.0). Sausalito ferry terminal to Waldo (first ~1.7 mi): OpenHistoricalMap way 200221493 (CC0, digitised from the USGS Tamalpais 1897 topographic sheet) - real but coarse, about one vertex per 150-300 m along the Sausalito waterfront, which has been built over. Waldo to Almonte, Alto tunnel, Corte Madera and Baltimore Park: OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=Northwestern Pacific Railroad (Mill Valley - Sausalito Path, Alto Tunnel, Corte Madera Pathway), i.e. the abandoned NWP grade itself. The Baltimore Park cutoff east along Corte Madera Creek to the old California Northwestern line at Greenbrae: OSM abandoned NWP grade (Corte Madera - Larkspur Path). Greenbrae through the Cal Park Hill tunnel to the San Rafael depot: the active SMART main line (OSM 'Mainline Subdivision'). LATER-ALIGNMENT CAVEAT: SMART relaid this section in 2010-2019 on the old NWP formation and through the original Cal Park tunnel, so the drawn line is the historic alignment carried by modern track, not a survey of the 1904-1941 track. No straight-line legs. Milepost check against the 1933 employee timetable (distances from San Francisco; Sausalito = 6.5): traced Almonte 10.0 (TT 9.9), San Rafael 17.1 (17.0).

segments.note: After Harriman brought the North Shore and the rival California Northwestern under common control in 1904, a cutoff was built east from Baltimore Park (Larkspur) to the CNW line at Greenbrae, and the CNW was electrified from there through the Cal Park tunnel to San Rafael, letting North Shore trains use the CNW station there. Wikipedia (citing Sievers 1954) gives the new route as opened in 1904; Sievers says only that 'by 1904' the lines into San Rafael were electrified - the opening month is not sourced. North Shore trains ran it until the 1907 merger into the Northwestern Pacific. Headway is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: opening year from Wikipedia citing Sievers, Western Railroader Aug 1954 (year only); headway is an estimate, not sourced.

segments.note: The North Shore was merged into the Northwestern Pacific Railroad in 1907 (jointly owned by the Southern Pacific and the Santa Fe until 1929), which ran the electric service from then on. The Mill Valley branch also fed the Mount Tamalpais and Muir Woods Railway, whose trains left from the Mill Valley depot. Headway is an ESTIMATE (ferry-timed, roughly half-hourly at peaks).

segments.note: The Santa Fe sold its half of the NWP to the Southern Pacific in 1929; the SP invested in the interurbans - new Mission-style suburban depots and steel cars (St. Louis Car Co., 1929-30) - but the 1929 Mill Valley fire, the Depression, a 1934 fare rise and the May 1937 opening of the Golden Gate Bridge drained traffic. The California Railroad Commission approved abandonment on 3 October 1939, a Marin municipal-utility-district takeover lost at the polls on 7 November 1939, and the last electric trains ran on 28 February 1941 (Sievers 1954; Wikipedia citing Trimble p.74). The 1929 brush fire in Mill Valley and the closure of the connecting Mount Tamalpais railway that year hit this branch hardest. NWP employee Time-Table No. 59 (Interurban Trains), effective 1 Feb 1933, read from the page scans: Mill Valley trains left every 30 min from about 5.45 to 9.45 am and hourly through the middle of the day, each timed to a Sausalito ferry.
sources: Segment-level: headway and running time read from NWP employee Time-Table No. 59, 1 Feb 1933 (the opening and closing dates from Wikipedia/Trimble and Sievers below).
